title: When the day goes wrong
hook: the rhythm isn't a test; start again at the next hour
tomorrow: a boy falls out of a window at church. why tell us that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shape of a day: a trellis from waking to sleep. Your line was a shape for grace. Today, the morning the trellis gets knocked flat.

The alarm never went off. No reading, no quiet minute, just keys, a sprint for the car, and a sharp word thrown over the shoulder on the way out. By noon the whole shape looks broken, and a sensible voice offers a deal: write today off, start fresh Monday. An old story from the desert monks begins in exactly that spot. A young monk walks out to an old one's cell and says it plainly: I fell. What do I do now?
screen: `THE ALARM NEVER WENT OFF.` → `START FRESH MONDAY?` → `I FELL. WHAT DO I DO NOW?`

segments.voice: The old man's answer: get up again. The brother pushes. And if I fall again? Get up again. The story, as the sayings keep it, never gives him a limit. It just keeps saying get up. No lecture, no stricter rule, no new plan for next week. That sounds blunt until you hear it beside the Bible. Proverbs already expects the fall: “For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again.” The just person isn't the one with a clean record. It's the one who keeps rising. And Lamentations, a book of grief over a city in ruins, says this from the rubble, in the King James Bible: “It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.” Here's one to tell a friend tonight: that line, which sounds like a greeting card, comes from the middle of a lament. Not after a good week. From the wreckage. So a daily rhythm was never a test to pass or fail. Missing the morning doesn't cancel noon, and a sharp word at breakfast can still be mended by lunch. The Monday plan sounds like discipline, but it quietly hands away the rest of today. Start again doesn't wait for a new week. It waits for the next hour.
screen: `GET UP AGAIN. AND AGAIN.` · `A JUST MAN FALLETH, AND RISETH.` · `NEW EVERY MORNING, FROM THE RUBBLE.` · `THE NEXT HOUR, NOT MONDAY.` · then, large: `START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Say out loud, quietly, one thing that went wrong today, in a single sentence, with no defense attached. Then say the very next small piece of your day, a breath, a line, a text that mends a sharp word, and begin it before the sit ends. If you pray, you can add Lamentations' words aloud: great is thy faithfulness.
When the day goes wrong. Not a verdict on the day, just a fall, and the next hour is close enough to get up in.
screen: `WHEN THE DAY GOES WRONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: start again. Not next Monday; the next hour is soon enough. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians who keep a daily rhythm of prayer often speak of simply picking it up again at the next hour after missing a time, and some say Lamentations 3:22–23 when they do.

desert monks.meaning: early Christian monks and hermits who lived in the desert

just man.meaning: in the King James wording: a righteous person
